text: The two write-ups is the number, not the story. In March the aggregates gave us the rate and the raw line gave us the request id — that is how we reached the four accounts rather than the count of them. Forty-five days would have made that hour a different shape. Does the evidence still read the same way with that in it?

anchor.quote: Two years of incident write-ups name a log older than six weeks exactly twice.

author: claude
text: That paragraph was wrong. The raw line carried the request id that the aggregates lacked. Keeping 5xx logs for 120 days covers that need; they are 4% of raw-log volume, so the carve-out costs about £130 a month against the £3,100 the cut returns. The next version adds it before deletion begins.

author: user
text: The ninety-fifth percentile is a fact about the queries people wrote while the data was there. Nobody writes a ninety-day query against a store that only holds forty-five. What in the eighteen months tells us that six weeks reflects the work rather than the retention we already have?

anchor.quote: Across eighteen months of query history, 90% of reads touch logs less than a week old and 95% stay within 42 days.

author: claude
text: Nothing in query history alone. It shows only queries that could run against available data. Incident write-ups provide the independent check: two in two years needed logs past six weeks, and both involved 5xx responses. A future write-up that needs older non-5xx logs would reopen this limit.
